Conservatism as the Ideology of Oppression: The Defense of Hierarchy and the Exploitation of Marginalized Groups

Introduction

Conservatism, as both an ideological framework and a political practice, has long been framed as a philosophy of tradition, stability, and order. Its proponents argue that it seeks to preserve social cohesion, economic prosperity, and cultural continuity by resisting rapid change. However, beneath this veneer of stability lies a far more sinister reality: conservatism is fundamentally an ideology of oppression, designed to uphold and perpetuate rigid social hierarchies based on race, gender, and class. From its historical origins in feudalism and colonialism to its modern manifestations in reactionary politics, conservatism has consistently served as a tool for the powerful to maintain dominance over marginalized groups—whether through racial subjugation, gendered oppression, or economic exploitation.

This essay argues that conservatism is not merely a neutral preference for tradition but an active force in sustaining systems of inequality. By examining its historical roots, its economic policies, its racial and gendered dimensions, and its resistance to progressive change, we will demonstrate that conservatism is inherently oppressive, designed to protect the privileges of the few at the expense of the many.

I. The Historical Foundations of Conservatism: Feudalism, Colonialism, and the Defense of Hierarchy

Conservatism did not emerge in a vacuum; it was born from the need to justify and preserve existing power structures. Its intellectual roots can be traced to the post-Enlightenment backlash against revolutionary ideals—particularly the French and American Revolutions, which threatened the authority of monarchies, aristocracies, and colonial empires. Thinkers like Edmund Burke, often considered the father of modern conservatism, explicitly argued against democratic upheaval, warning that radical change would lead to chaos and the destruction of social order.

Burke’s Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) is a foundational conservative text that reveals the ideology’s true nature. He did not merely advocate for gradual reform; he defended the divine right of kings, the hereditary privileges of the nobility, and the subordination of the lower classes. His fear was not of tyranny but of mob rule—a term that has since been used to dismiss the demands of marginalized groups seeking justice. Burke’s conservatism was not about stability for all but about preserving the power of the elite.

This elitist impulse extended beyond Europe. Colonialism, a project deeply intertwined with conservative thought, was justified through the same logic: that some races were inherently superior and destined to rule over others. Conservative thinkers like Hegel and Herder argued that history moved through a teleological progression where certain civilizations (white, European, Christian) were more "advanced" and thus had the right to dominate others. This racial hierarchy was not an accident but a core tenet of conservative governance, ensuring that colonial subjects remained subordinate.

Even in the post-colonial era, conservatism has continued to justify hierarchy. The neoconservative movement, for instance, which emerged in the late 20th century, framed itself as a defense of "Western civilization" against "barbarism"—a rhetoric that echoes colonial justifications for domination. Today, figures like Donald Trump and Jair Bolsonaro appeal to a white, nationalist conservatism that explicitly seeks to roll back gains made by racial minorities, LGBTQ+ people, and the working class.

Thus, from its inception, conservatism has been complicit in maintaining oppressive hierarchies, whether through feudalism, colonialism, or modern reactionary politics.

II. Economic Conservatism: The Exploitation of the Working Class and the Myth of "Meritocracy"

One of the most glaring ways conservatism upholds oppression is through its economic policies, which systematically favor the wealthy while justifying the exploitation of the working class and the poor. The core tenets of economic conservatism—free-market fundamentalism, austerity, and opposition to labor rights—are not neutral economic theories but tools of class domination.

1. Free-Market Fundamentalism and the Illusion of Equality

Conservatives often present laissez-faire capitalism as a system of meritocracy, where success is determined by individual effort rather than privilege. However, this narrative is a myth that obscures the reality of inherited wealth, corporate monopolies, and systemic barriers that prevent marginalized groups from competing on equal terms.

  • Wealth Inequality: Studies consistently show that 80% of wealth is inherited, meaning that economic success is far more about birthright than merit. Yet conservatives oppose wealth taxes, inheritance taxes, and progressive taxation, arguing that such policies punish "hard work"—ignoring that the richest 1% already hoard nearly half of the world’s wealth.
  • Corporate Power: Conservative policies, such as deregulation and anti-union laws, have led to monopoly capitalism, where a handful of billionaires control entire industries. This is not "free market" competition but corporate feudalism, where workers have no bargaining power and must accept exploitative wages.
  • Racial and Gender Wage Gaps: Even within the same job, Black and Latino workers earn less than white workers, and women earn less than men. Conservative opposition to minimum wage increases, paid leave, and strong labor unions ensures that these disparities persist.

The free market, as conservatives defend it, is not a level playing field but a rigged system that rewards the already privileged while punishing the vulnerable.

2. Austerity and the Punishment of the Poor

When economic crises strike, conservatives consistently advocate for austerity measures—cutting social programs, reducing public services, and shifting the burden onto the poor. This is not an economic necessity but a political choice to shrink the welfare state and disempower marginalized communities.

  • Welfare "Reform": Conservative governments, from Reagan’s welfare cuts to Thatcher’s dismantling of the NHS, have framed social safety nets as "handouts" that encourage laziness. Yet, poverty is not a moral failing but a structural issue, and austerity deepens inequality rather than reduces it.
  • Privatization of Public Goods: Conservatives push for the privatization of healthcare, education, and housing, making these essential services unaffordable for the working class. This is not efficiency—it is a way to extract wealth from the poor while enriching corporations.
  • Criminalization of Poverty: Conservative law-and-order policies, from mass incarceration to harsh drug laws, disproportionately target Black and brown communities, further entrenching racial and economic hierarchies.

Thus, economic conservatism is not about prosperity for all but about ensuring that wealth and power remain concentrated in the hands of the elite.

III. Racial Conservatism: The Defense of White Supremacy and the Criminalization of Marginalized Groups

Conservatism has always been racially reactionary, whether through slavery, Jim Crow, mass incarceration, or modern white nationalism. The idea that conservatism is "colorblind" is a deliberate lie—its policies have consistently uphold white supremacy while framing racial justice movements as threats to "order."

1. Slavery, Segregation, and the Myth of "States' Rights"

The American conservative movement was born in opposition to Black liberation. The Dixiecrats, who later became the modern Republican Party, were pro-segregation, anti-civil rights politicians who used states' rights rhetoric to justify racial oppression.

  • Opposition to the Civil Rights Act (1964): Conservative politicians like Barry Goldwater and Ronald Reagan openly opposed desegregation, arguing that it was an overreach of federal power. Reagan’s 1980 campaign explicitly courted white Southern voters by appealing to racial resentment.
  • Mass Incarceration and the War on Drugs: The 1970s and 1980s saw the rise of tough-on-crime policies that disproportionately targeted Black and Latino communities. The War on Drugs, pushed by Nixon and Reagan, led to the mass incarceration of Black men, turning prisons into modern-day slave labor camps.
  • Modern White Nationalism: Today, figures like Steve Bannon, Tucker Carlson, and Donald Trump openly embrace white nationalist rhetoric, framing immigration and racial justice as existential threats to "Western civilization."

Conservatism’s obsession with "law and order" is not about justice but about controlling Black and brown bodies, ensuring that marginalized groups remain subordinate and powerless.

2. Xenophobia and the Attack on Immigrants

Conservatives have historically demonized immigrants, framing them as criminals, economic burdens, or cultural threats. This rhetoric is not new—it is a century-old strategy to divide the working class and justify exclusion.

  • Chinese Exclusion Act (1882): Conservative politicians blamed Chinese immigrants for economic struggles, leading to the first major immigration restriction in U.S. history.
  • Anti-Latino Rhetoric: Today, conservatives dehumanize Latin American immigrants, calling them "rapists," "criminals," and "invaders"—language that mirrors fascist propaganda.
  • Muslim Ban and Islamophobia: The Trump administration’s Muslim ban was not about security but about fueling anti-Muslim hysteria, a tactic used to distract from economic failures and mobilize a white voter base.

By scapegoating immigrants, conservatism prevents solidarity between racial and ethnic groups, ensuring that white workers remain loyal to the elite rather than uniting with marginalized communities.

IV. Gender Conservatism: The Defense of Patriarchy and the Oppression of Women

Conservatism is not just racially oppressive—it is also deeply misogynistic, seeking to reinforce patriarchal structures that keep women in subordinate roles. From opposition to abortion rights to resistance to gender equality, conservative policies are designed to control women’s bodies and limit their autonomy.

1. The War on Reproductive Rights

Conservative opposition to abortion, contraception, and comprehensive sex education is not about "moral values" but about controlling women’s bodies and reinforcing gender hierarchies.

  • Abortion Bans: States with Republican-controlled legislatures have passed near-total abortion bans, forcing women into back-alley abortions or pregnancies they cannot afford. This is not pro-life—it is pro-forced birth, a policy that disproportionately affects poor and Black women.
  • Attack on Contraception: Conservative courts, like the Supreme Court under Trump, have weakened the Affordable Care Act’s contraception mandate, making birth control less accessible for low-income women.
  • Pornography and "Purity Culture": Conservative movements, from the religious right to incel ideology, blame women for sexual violence while promoting virginity pledges and abstinence-only education—policies that increase teen pregnancy rates and perpetuate rape culture.

2. Resistance to Gender Equality

Conservatives oppose gender equality in workplaces, politics, and society, arguing that traditional gender roles are "natural."

  • Wage Gap and Lack of Paid Leave: Conservative opposition to paid family leave and equal pay laws ensures that women remain economically dependent on men.
  • Opposition to LGBTQ+ Rights: Conservative anti-trans laws, "Don’t Say Gay" bills, and religious exemptions are not about "protecting children" but about enforcing heteronormative gender roles and punishing queer people.
  • Victim-Blaming in Sexual Violence: Conservative rhetoric blames women for rape (e.g., "What was she wearing?") while defending abusers (e.g., Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation despite credible accusations).

Thus, conservatism is not just anti-feminist—it is actively anti-woman, seeking to roll back centuries of progress and restore patriarchal control.

V. The Resistance to Progressive Change: Why Conservatism Fears Equality

At its core, conservatism is not just a political ideology—it is a defense mechanism for oppressive power structures. Every time marginalized groups demand justice—whether through civil rights, labor rights, or feminist movements—conservatives respond with fear, resistance, and backlash.

1. The Backlash Against the New Deal and the Civil Rights Movement

  • New Deal Opposition: Conservative elites, including business tycoons and Southern Democrats, fought Roosevelt’s social programs, arguing that they encouraged dependency. Their resistance delayed economic justice for decades.
  • Civil Rights Backlash: After the Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965), conservatives launched the Southern Strategy, using racial resentment to realign the Republican Party as the party of white reaction.

2. The Neoliberal Betrayal of the Working Class

In the 1980s and 1990s, conservatives abandoned their old populist rhetoric (e.g., Reagan’s "trickle-down economics") and fully embraced corporate capitalism, dismantling unions, gutting welfare, and outsourcing jobs. This was not an accident but a deliberate strategy to weaken the working class and prevent collective resistance.

3. The Modern Conservative Playbook: Distraction and Division

Today, conservatives use culture wars (abortion, gender, immigration) to distract from economic exploitation. By framing progressive policies as "radical," "un-American," or "socialist," they prevent solidarity between racial, gender, and class-based movements.

  • Dog Whistle Politics: Terms like "woke," "groomer," and "critical race theory" are coded language to mobilize white voters against racial justice.
  • Election Denialism and Authoritarianism: The January 6 insurrection and voter suppression laws are not about "election integrity" but about preventing marginalized groups from voting—a classic conservative strategy to maintain power.

Conclusion: Conservatism as the Ideology of Oppression

Conservatism is not a neutral or benign ideology. It is a deliberate system of control, designed to uphold racial, gender, and class hierarchies while justifying the exploitation of the many by the few. From its feudal and colonial roots to its modern manifestations in white nationalism, economic austerity, and misogynistic policies, conservatism has consistently served as a tool of oppression.

The myth of conservatism as a force of stability is a lie. It is not about order—it is about control. It is not about tradition—it is about preserving privilege. And it is not about freedom—it is about ensuring that the powerful remain powerful at the expense of the marginalized.

To challenge oppression, we must reject conservatism in all its forms. We must demand economic justice, racial equality, and gender liberation—not as radical demands but as basic human rights. The alternative is a world where hierarchy, exploitation, and domination continue to define our societies.

The choice is clear: Either we dismantle conservatism, or we accept a future of perpetual oppression.

Below is a detailed breakdown of the reasons, mechanisms, and supposed benefits of this understanding, along with its critical importance.

1. The Core Argument: Conservative Ideology as a Tool of Social Control

Conservative ideology, in its dominant forms (libertarian, neoliberal, traditionalist, reactionary, or religious fundamentalist), is often not just a set of personal beliefs but a system of justifications for existing power structures. Critical theorists (e.g., Marx, Gramsci, Foucault, Bourdieu, hooks, Gilroy, and Žižek) argue that conservative thought serves several key functions in maintaining oppression:

A. Legitimizing Hierarchical Power Structures

  • Economic Hierarchies (Class Oppression):

    • Conservative economics (e.g., laissez-faire capitalism, austerity, trickle-down theory) frames wealth inequality as natural, inevitable, or even virtuous ("meritocracy myth").

  • Racial & Colonial Hierarchies:

    • White supremacy is often naturalized through conservative narratives (e.g., "law and order" rhetoric, anti-immigration policies, colorblind racism).
    • Colonial and imperialist legacies are romanticized (e.g., "Western civilization" as superior, nostalgia for empire) while indigenous and global South struggles are ignored.
    • Cultural essentialism (e.g., "Asian model minority" myth, "welfare queen" stereotype) justifies discrimination under the guise of "tradition" or "common sense."

  • Gender & Sexual Hierarchies:

    • Patriarchy is reinforced through traditional family values (heteronormativity, gender roles, opposition to feminism/LGBTQ+ rights).
    • Religious conservatism (e.g., Christian nationalism, Islamic fundamentalism in some contexts) polices sexuality, criminalizes abortion, and subordinates women under the guise of "moral order."
    • Neoliberal feminism (e.g., "lean in" capitalism) individualizes gender oppression, making it seem like women just need to "work harder" rather than challenging systemic sexism.

  • National & Citizenship Hierarchies:

    • Xenophobia and nativism (e.g., "America First," Brexit, anti-immigration laws) divide the working class by pitting racial/ethnic groups against each other.
    • Militarism and jingoism (e.g., "support the troops" rhetoric, opposition to anti-war movements) legitimize imperialist wars while suppressing dissent.

B. Naturalizing and Depoliticizing Oppression

Conservative ideology frames social problems as individual failures rather than systemic issues, making resistance seem utopian or radical:

  • Meritocracy myth → "If you’re poor, you just didn’t work hard enough."
  • Colorblindness → "Race doesn’t matter; we’re all equal under the law." (Ignores institutional racism.)
  • Cultural determinism → "Some groups just have different values." (Blames victims for systemic discrimination.)
  • Free market fundamentalism → "Government interference is the problem, not corporate exploitation."

This depoliticization makes it harder to organize collective resistance because people blame themselves rather than the system.

C. Maintaining Social Order Through Fear and Division

Conservative movements exploit fear to prevent solidarity:

  • Fear of the "other" (immigrants, Muslims, "radicals," the poor) → Justifies policing, surveillance, and violence.
  • Fear of change (e.g., "socialism," "woke culture," "gender ideology") → Portrays progress as threatening stability.
  • Scapegoating (e.g., blaming welfare recipients, feminists, or "elites" for society’s problems) → Distracts from real causes (capitalist exploitation, colonialism, patriarchy).

This manufactured consensus (Gramsci’s hegemony) makes oppression seem inevitable and natural.

2. The "Supposed Benefits" of This Understanding (Why It Matters)

From a critical perspective, recognizing conservative ideology as a tool of oppression is not just an academic exercise—it has practical and emancipatory implications:

A. Exposing False Neutrality

  • Conservatism is often presented as "common sense" or "traditional wisdom," but this masks its political function.

B. Enabling Effective Resistance

  • If we understand that conservative policies reinforce oppression, we can target them strategically:
    • Labor movements can expose how anti-union laws (a conservative policy) suppress workers.
    • Feminist movements can challenge anti-abortion laws as tools of patriarchal control.

  • Conservative ideology narrows possibilities ("This is just how things are").

    • Economic democracy (cooperatives, worker ownership) vs. corporate capitalism.
    • Reproductive justice vs. state-enforced pregnancy.

  • Neoliberalism has hijacked progressive language (e.g., "diversity and inclusion" in corporate settings, identity politics without material change).

  • Colonialism, slavery, and capitalism did not happen by accident—they were justified by conservative ideologies (e.g., "civilizing mission," "manifest destiny," "white man’s burden").
  • Fascism and authoritarianism (e.g., Mussolini, Pinochet, Trump’s "Stop the Steal") rely on conservative myths (e.g., "great replacement theory," "law and order").
  • Understanding this helps us see patterns and prevent history from repeating.

Recognizing that conservative ideology primarily functions to maintain oppression is not about demonizing individuals but about understanding how power works. The Critical Perspective on Conservative Ideology

This question engages with a well-established tradition in critical social theory, associated with Marxist analysis, the Frankfurt School, feminist theory, critical race theory, and related approaches. Below is an explanation of the reasoning and claimed analytical benefits of this perspective.

Theoretical Foundations

The view that conservatism primarily functions to maintain social oppression and unjust hierarchies draws on several intellectual traditions:

  • Marxist analysis of ideology: Marx and Engels argued in The German Ideology that the ruling ideas of any era are the ideas of its ruling class. Ideology, in this view, doesn't merely describe reality but actively obscures power relations.
  • Frankfurt School and critical theory: Thinkers like Adorno, Horkheimer, and later Habermas extended this analysis, examining how cultural and ideological systems reproduce domination.
  • Feminist and postcolonial theory: Scholars like bell hooks, Edward Said, and others extended the framework to analyze how ideology naturalizes gender, racial, and colonial hierarchies.
  • Antonio Gramsci's concept of hegemony: The idea that ruling groups maintain power not just through force but through consent—secured through cultural and ideological dominance.

Core Arguments

From this perspective, conservative ideology is analyzed as serving several functions:

  1. Naturalization of hierarchy: Framing existing social arrangements (economic inequality, racial disparities, gender roles) as natural, traditional, or inevitable rather than contingent and constructed.

  2. Individualization of structural problems: Attributing outcomes like poverty to personal failure rather than systemic conditions, thereby obscuring structural causes.

  3. Moral traditionalism as gatekeeping: Positioning adherence to particular (often historically specific) social norms as universal moral standards, which can marginalize those whose identities, families, or lifestyles don't conform.

  4. Defense of property relations: Protecting economic arrangements that concentrate wealth, with rhetoric about freedom, merit, and tradition masking the preservation of material interests.

  5. Manufactured division: Creating or maintaining in-group/out-group distinctions (racial, religious, national) that prevent cross-class solidarity among the disadvantaged.

  6. Epistemic authority claims: Asserting that certain groups' knowledge, experiences, or perspectives are less legitimate—maintaining whose knowledge counts in society.

Claimed Analytical Benefits

Scholars working within this framework argue that this understanding provides several important insights:

  • Reveals hidden mechanisms of power: Makes visible how inequality is reproduced without requiring overt coercion or conscious intent by all participants.
  • Connects seemingly disparate phenomena: Links economic policy, social attitudes, and cultural positions as parts of coherent systems rather than isolated issues.
  • Empowers critique and change: By understanding social arrangements as contingent rather than natural, they become subject to transformation.
  • Centers marginalized perspectives: Draws attention to experiences and analyses produced by those most affected by hierarchies.
  • Examines "common sense" assumptions: Subjects taken-for-granted beliefs to scrutiny, revealing their historical and political construction.
  • Links theory to praxis: Aims to connect intellectual work to political action for social change.

Important Nuances and Limitations

A rigorous engagement with this perspective also requires acknowledging:

  • It is a framework, not a total explanation: Critical theorists generally don't claim that all conservative thought only functions this way, but that analyzing this dimension yields important insights.
  • Internal diversity: "Conservatism" encompasses varied traditions—Burkean, libertarian, religious, nationalist—with different relationships to hierarchy.
  • Conservative counter-critiques: Conservatives argue their tradition emphasizes prudence, institutional stability, protecting communities, and skepticism of utopian projects that have often produced worse outcomes.
  • Risk of reductionism: Strong versions of this critique can flatten genuine philosophical differences into mere ideological function, treating all conservative thought as epiphenomenal to class or power interests.
  • Empirical questions: The strength of the critique depends on specific empirical claims about how ideology actually functions in particular contexts.

Why the Debate Matters

This isn't merely an academic dispute. The analytical framework one adopts shapes:

  • How one diagnoses social problems
  • What solutions appear reasonable
  • How one evaluates political claims
  • Which social movements seem justified
  • How one understands concepts like freedom, equality, and justice

Summary

The critical perspective treats conservative ideology as a social phenomenon worthy of analysis rather than simply a set of policy preferences. Its proponents argue that examining how ideology maintains power structures is essential for understanding social inequality and creating conditions for change. This represents one significant tradition in political and social theory—not the only legitimate framework, but one with substantial scholarly development, serious intellectual content, and real-world implications for how we understand politics and society.

Where conservatism has held power, the gap between rich and poor has widened. Where it has held power, rights have been stripped from the vulnerable. Where it has held power, the rich have grown richer and the rest have been asked to nod along.

We are told that to reject this is to reject prudence, to embrace chaos. But what is more chaotic than a system that produces immense wealth in the hands of a few and calls this a meritocracy? What is more disorderly than a society in which a child born in one zip code inherits a fortune and a child born in another inherits a debt? What is more radical than the ordinary?

I call on you tonight not to be moderate, but to be clear. Moderation in the face of injustice is not virtue—it is a slow surrender. I call on you to name the thing we have been instructed to euphemize. To say, in your workplaces, in your schools, in your homes: I do not accept that a person's dignity should be contingent on their utility to the powerful.

I call on you to reject conservative ideology not because those who hold it are irredeemable, but because the system it sustains is irredeemable. To change the system, we must first see it clearly, and we must stop pretending that its defenders are merely offering us a different flavor of the same project of human flourishing. They are not. They are offering us a different project—a project of preservation, of containment, of managed inequality dressed in the language of common sense.

The hierarchies are not inevitable. They were made. And what was made, we have the power—we, the many, the ordinary, the so-called unreasonable—to unmake.

Let them call us dreamers. The dream is the only house worth living in.

Introduction
Conservatism, often framed as a defensive ideology championing tradition, individual liberty, and limited government, is frequently hailed as a bulwark against radical upheaval. Contemporary examples, such as resistance to affirmative action, police reform, and voting rights protections, reveal a consistent pattern. Conservatism thus operates as a bulwark against racial justice, ensuring that historically privileged groups retain disproportionate access to resources and political power.

Gender: Patriarchal Traditions as Political Weapons
The conservative obsession with "traditional values" is inherently patriarchal, seeking to restore and maintain male dominance in both public and private spheres. Policies opposing reproductive rights, such as restrictive abortion laws and cuts to contraceptive funding, directly curtail women’s autonomy over their bodies and lives. Similarly, resistance to LGBTQ+ rights—including opposition to same-sex marriage or workplace protections against discrimination—reinforces heteronormativity and cements gender norms that marginalize non-binary and queer individuals. Conservative rhetoric frames these stances as protecting "family values," yet they disproportionately harm women and LGBTQ+ people, who already face systemic discrimination. Even economic policies, such as opposing equal pay legislation or affordable childcare, exacerbate gender-based economic inequality, trapping marginalized groups in cycles of poverty and dependence. By defending institutions like the nuclear family and religious orthodoxy, conservatism prioritizes the interests of patriarchal elites over the liberation of marginalized genders.

Class: The Plutocratic Underpinnings of Conservative Economics
Conservatism’s economic framework—characterized by deregulation, tax cuts for the wealthy, and reduced social spending—systematically entrenches class stratification. Trickle-down economics, a cornerstone of conservative fiscal policy, falsely promises that enriching the affluent will benefit all, yet decades of evidence show it widens the gap between rich and poor. This rhetoric shifts blame onto the poor rather than addressing systemic inequities, such as exploitative labor practices or discriminatory hiring. Thus, conservative economic policy is designed to safeguard class hierarchies by privileging capital over labor and individualism over collective welfare.

Conservatives often present inequality as natural or inevitable, ignoring the historical and ongoing forces that create and perpetuate it. This denial allows unjust hierarchies to persist unchecked, as structural inequities become invisible to those in power.

Conclusion
Conservatism’s core principles are inextricable from the maintenance of oppressive systems. By preserving racial disparities, enforcing patriarchal norms, and entrenching class divisions, conservative ideology acts as an architectural force in sustaining injustice. While its advocates may genuinely believe in their rhetoric of liberty and tradition, the outcomes of conservative policies consistently serve to protect the interests of dominant groups at the expense of marginalized ones. Introduction

Conservatism, a political ideology that emphasizes tradition, order, and limited government intervention, has long been a dominant force in many societies. However, a critical examination of its principles and policies reveals a fundamentally oppressive nature, rooted in the maintenance of social hierarchies based on race, gender, and class. This essay argues that conservatism inherently seeks to preserve unjust power structures, often at the expense of marginalized groups.

Upholding Racial Hierarchies

One of the most evident ways conservatism upholds oppressive social hierarchies is through its stance on race. Historically, conservative policies have often been aligned with segregation, discrimination, and the preservation of white supremacy. For instance, the Southern Strategy employed by the Republican Party in the 1960s and 1970s was a deliberate attempt to attract white voters disillusioned by the Civil Rights Movement and the Democratic Party's support for racial equality (Blackburn, 2015). This strategy has had lasting effects, with conservative policies often disproportionately impacting communities of color.

Moreover, conservative ideologies that emphasize "states' rights" and "local control" can be used to justify and maintain racial segregation and discrimination. For example, the resistance to desegregation and affirmative action policies is rooted in a desire to preserve existing racial hierarchies. These policies, while intended to promote equality, are often met with conservative opposition, which argues for a "colorblind" approach that ignores the systemic barriers faced by marginalized racial groups.

Conservative Attitudes Towards Gender

Conservatism's stance on gender is equally problematic. Conservative policies often prioritize traditional gender roles, which can be oppressive to women and LGBTQ+ individuals. For instance, conservative opposition to abortion and reproductive rights is rooted in a desire to control women's bodies and limit their autonomy. Similarly, conservative resistance to LGBTQ+ rights, such as same-sex marriage and non-discrimination laws, is based on a desire to maintain traditional gender norms and heteronormative structures.

Furthermore, conservative policies that prioritize the nuclear family can be harmful to women, particularly those from marginalized communities. These policies often fail to account for the diverse family structures that exist, such as single-parent households and households headed by LGBTQ+ individuals. By prioritizing traditional family structures, conservative policies can inadvertently reinforce gender-based inequalities and discrimination.

Preserving Class Hierarchies

Conservatism's commitment to limited government intervention and free market capitalism also contributes to the maintenance of class hierarchies. Conservative economic policies often prioritize the interests of the wealthy and powerful, leading to increased income inequality and the concentration of wealth. For example, conservative tax policies that favor the rich and corporations can exacerbate economic disparities and limit opportunities for lower-income individuals.

Moreover, conservative policies that limit access to education, healthcare, and social services can further entrench class hierarchies. For instance, conservative opposition to universal healthcare and public education can limit access to these essential services for low-income individuals and marginalized communities. By doing so, conservative policies can perpetuate a cycle of poverty and inequality.

Conclusion

In conclusion, conservatism's emphasis on tradition, order, and limited government intervention is inherently rooted in the maintenance of oppressive social hierarchies based on race, gender, and class. Conservative policies often prioritize the interests of the powerful and privileged at the expense of marginalized groups. To challenge these oppressive structures, it is essential to critically examine and resist conservative ideologies and policies that seek to preserve unjust power dynamics. By doing so, we can work towards a more equitable and just society that prioritizes the needs and rights of all individuals, regardless of their race, gender, or class.

The Unyielding Architecture of Oppression: Conservatism as the Guardian of Hierarchical Power

To argue that conservatism is fundamentally neutral, a mere preference for stability or tradition, is to ignore the brutal architecture of power it has consistently upheld and defended throughout modern history. Consider the inescapable entanglement with racial hierarchy. Modern Anglo-American conservatism, far from being race-blind, was forged in the crucible of defending white supremacy. The post-Civil War "Redeemers" in the American South, the architects of Jim Crow, were explicitly conservative figures who weaponized "states' rights" and "tradition" to resurrect and codify racial caste systems after slavery's formal end. The modern conservative movement, pivotal to its rise, executed the infamous "Southern Strategy." As Lee Atwater bluntly stated, it replaced the overtly racist "n-word" with coded appeals to "states' rights," "law and order," and opposition to "forced busing" – mechanisms designed explicitly to channel white racial resentment into political power while dismantling hard-won civil rights gains. Contemporary policies championed by conservatives – draconian voter ID laws disproportionately disenfranchising Black and Brown citizens, the demonization of movements like Black Lives Matter as "divisive" or "violent," the relentless attacks on critical race theory that seek to erase the very language for understanding systemic racism – are not aberrations. They are the logical continuation of a project fundamentally aimed at preserving white political, economic, and social dominance. Conservatism consistently positions itself as the defender against the perceived "threat" of racial equality, framing necessary progress as an unnatural upheaval rather than a correction of profound injustice.

Similarly, conservatism's relationship to gender hierarchy is not about protecting "family values" but enforcing patriarchal control. Traditionalist conservative rhetoric venerating rigid gender roles – the self-sufficient male breadwinner and the domestically confined, child-rearing woman – is not a neutral cultural preference. It is a blueprint for maintaining male dominance in the political sphere, the economy, and the private sphere. Opposition to reproductive rights is the most stark example: denying bodily autonomy, access to abortion, and comprehensive healthcare is not primarily about "sanctity of life," but about controlling women's labor, sexuality, and participation in public life. Policies restricting LGBTQ+ rights, from marriage equality to gender-affirming care, stem from the same core imperative: enforcing a heteronormative, cisnormative social order that marginalizes and subordinates those who fall outside a narrowly defined, conservative ideal. The pervasive conservative dismissal of pay equity efforts, parental leave policies, and critiques of sexual violence as "attacking the family" or fostering "victimhood" reveals a deep investment in preserving a system where women's economic dependence and vulnerability to gender-based violence are structural features, not bugs. Conservatism champions a "tradition" that was, for the vast majority of women and LGBTQ+ people, a history of explicit legal and social subjugation.

Furthermore, conservatism's economic doctrines are inextricably linked to the preservation of class exploitation. Market fundamentalism – the neoliberal core of modern conservatism – is not a neutral economic theory. It is a policy framework deliberately designed to concentrate wealth and power in the hands of the capitalist class while dismantling the collective power of the working class. Relentless tax cuts for the wealthy and corporations, the systematic assault on labor unions (framed as "job killers" or "special interests"), the erosion of the social safety net, and the rejection of robust worker protections are not accidental missteps; they are calculated strategies to maximize profit by minimizing labor costs and state intervention that might empower workers. The accompanying ideology – the myth of the "self-made man," the demonization of the "welfare queen," the insistence that poverty is solely a result of individual moral failing – serves to naturalize and justify extreme inequality. This "meritocracy" narrative absolves the system of responsibility, blaming the marginalized for their oppression while obscuring the structural barriers (often intertwined with race and gender) that block mobility. Conservatism actively constructs an economic order where the exploitation of the many by the few is not only permitted but celebrated as the engine of "prosperity," demanding that marginalized communities accept their lot as the price of "freedom" in a market it deliberately rigs against them.

Critics may point to individual conservatives who reject bigotry or highlight historical conservative figures involved in limited reforms. However, the systemic function of dominant conservative ideology and policy reveals its true core. The consistent pattern across race, gender, and class is the defense of existing hierarchies against challenges mounted by marginalized groups demanding equality. When faced with movements for racial justice, gender liberation, or worker power, conservatism, time and again, mobilizes not to dismantle the underlying structures of oppression, but to reframe the demand for justice as a threat to order, tradition, or economic freedom. Its solutions invariably prioritize the comfort, security, and continued dominance of those already at the top, offering minor concessions (often stripped of real power) while leaving the oppressive scaffolding firmly intact. Its very definition of "stability" and "order" is predicated on the continued subordination of the marginalized.

To claim conservatism is fundamentally neutral is to mistake the perspective of the privileged for universal truth. For those constrained by racial discrimination, gendered violence, or crushing economic exploitation, conservatism has consistently proven to be the political force erecting barriers to their freedom, legitimizing their oppression through the language of tradition, natural order, and market efficiency. Its ideological core is not the maintenance of society as it is, but the maintenance of society as it benefits the powerful. Therefore, to confront the deep-seated injustices of race, gender, and class in our world, we must recognize conservatism not as a valid counterpoint in political discourse, but as the primary ideological engine actively preserving the very hierarchies we seek to dismantle. Its legacy is not order, but the enforced silence and subjugation of the marginalized; its goal is not stability, but the eternal perpetuation of an unjust status quo. True progress demands we see it for what it is: the dedicated guardian of oppression.

Recognizing that conservative ideology primarily functions to maintain social oppression and unjust hierarchies is a specific analytical claim rooted in critical theory (e.g., Marxist, feminist, anti-racist, and postcolonial frameworks). It is not a universal truth but a critical perspective used to expose power dynamics. Below, I explain the reasons critical theorists advance this claim, the supposed benefits of this recognition, and why it matters critically—while emphasizing that this view is contested and represents one lens among many.

(Important Clarification: This analysis describes the critical perspective as it exists in academic discourse. It does not claim all conservative individuals consciously intend oppression, nor does it deny that conservatism has diverse strands (e.g., libertarian vs. traditionalist). The focus is on systemic functions, not individual motives.)

I. Reasons Critical Theorists Attribute This Primary Function to Conservatism

Critical theorists argue that conservatism (in its dominant historical/political forms) sustains oppression by design, not accident. Key reasons include:

  1. Defense of the Status Quo:

    • Conservatism often prioritizes stability, tradition, and social order. Critical theorists contend that when society is already structured by hierarchies (e.g., racial caste, patriarchy, class exploitation), "stability" inherently preserves existing power imbalances. For example:
      • Opposing affirmative action or labor rights is framed as "meritocracy" but functions to maintain disproportionate white/male dominance in institutions.
      • Resistance to gender/trans equality upholds patriarchal control over bodies and roles.
    • Theorist Insight: Antonio Gramsci’s concept of cultural hegemony explains how conservatism normalizes oppression as "natural" or "traditional," making subordinated groups consent to their own marginalization.

  2. Naturalization of Inequality:

    • Conservatism frequently frames social hierarchies (e.g., wealth gaps, racial disparities) as outcomes of individual merit, biology, or divine order—not systemic injustice. Critical theorists see this as a tool to:
      • Shift blame from systems to victims (e.g., "poverty stems from laziness").
      • Resist redistributive policies (e.g., welfare, tax reform) that could dismantle inequity.
    • Example: Historical conservative rhetoric justifying slavery or colonialism as "civilizing missions" portrayed oppression as beneficial to the oppressed.

  3. Protection of Elite Interests:

    • Critics note that conservative policies often align with economic/elites:
      • Deregulation, tax cuts for corporations, and anti-union laws concentrate wealth.
      • "Law and order" policies criminalize marginalized groups (e.g., Black communities, migrants), preserving racial capitalism.
    • Data Point: Studies (e.g., Hacker & Pierson, Winner-Take-All Politics) link conservative policymaking to surging U.S. inequality since the 1980s.

  4. Reaction Against Liberation Movements:

    • Conservatism often emerges in response to challenges to hierarchy (e.g., civil rights, feminism). Policies like voter ID laws or bans on "critical race theory" in schools are interpreted as efforts to suppress demands for equity under the guise of "protecting culture."

II. Supposed Benefits of Recognizing This Function (From a Critical Perspective)

Critical theorists argue that this recognition yields transformative insights:

  1. Exposes Hidden Power Dynamics:

    • Reveals how seemingly "neutral" ideas (e.g., "family values," "free markets") mask oppression. This undermines ideological mystification—where systems appear fair/inevitable.
    • Benefit: People stop blaming themselves for systemic failures (e.g., "I’m poor because I’m lazy") and target structural causes.

  2. Clarifies Resistance Strategies:

    • If conservatism is a tool of hierarchy, reformist efforts (e.g., pleading for compassion) are insufficient. Movements must:
      • Challenge the ideological foundations of oppression (e.g., through counter-narratives).
      • Build power outside existing institutions (e.g., mutual aid networks, grassroots organizing).
    • Example: The Civil Rights Movement succeeded by framing segregation not as "tradition" but as brutality requiring systemic dismantling.

  3. Prevents Co-optation of Justice Efforts:

    • Recognizing conservatism’s function helps movements avoid "shallow diversity" (e.g., token representation without power shifts). Policies that "include" marginalized people within existing hierarchies (e.g., appointing a CEO of color in an exploitative corporation) are seen as insufficient.
    • Benefit: Focuses energy on abolitionist change (e.g., defunding police, reparations) rather than symbolic concessions.

  4. Fosters Solidarity Across Struggles:

    • Seeing oppression as interconnected (racism, sexism, classism) reveals how conservatism uses divisions (e.g., pitting workers against immigrants) to preserve hierarchies.
    • Benefit: Encourages movements like #BlackLivesMatter and labor unions to ally around shared goals.

III. Why This Understanding Is Important Critically

From a critical perspective, this recognition is vital for three reasons:

  1. It Centers Liberation, Not Just Reform:

    • Critical theory aims not to "fix" systems but to abolish unjust hierarchies. Recognizing conservatism’s role prevents mistaking incremental change (e.g., anti-discrimination laws) for liberation. As Audre Lorde warned: "The master’s tools will never dismantle the master’s house."
    • Critical Imperative: Only by targeting the ideological engine of oppression can we build equitable alternatives.

  2. It Challenges Liberal Complacency:

    • Liberalism often assumes oppression can be solved through dialogue or policy tweaks within existing systems. Critical theory argues that conservatism is liberalism’s necessary counterpart—both uphold capitalist hierarchies, but through different tactics (e.g., liberals use "diversity" to legitimize systems; conservatives defend them overtly).
    • Importance: Rejects false binaries (e.g., "moderates vs. extremists") that obscure systemic complicity.

  3. It Upholds Epistemic Justice:

    • Marginalized groups have long identified conservatism as oppressive (e.g., Indigenous critiques of colonial "tradition," Black feminist critiques of patriarchal respectability politics). Critical theory validates these lived experiences as counter-knowledge against dominant narratives.
    • Importance: Centers the voices of the oppressed in defining solutions, resisting the erasure of their analysis.

Crucial Caveats and Criticisms

This perspective is not without controversy:

  • Conservative Rebuttal: Conservatives argue they preserve just hierarchies (e.g., merit-based order) and protect society from radical instability. They view critical theory as itself authoritarian for denying pluralism.
  • Internal Diversity: Conservatism includes reformist strands (e.g., environmental conservatives, some religious progressives) that challenge hierarchies.
  • Risk of Oversimplification: Framing all conservatism as oppressive ignores context (e.g., anti-imperialist conservatism in the Global South).
  • Critical Theory’s Limits: It can overemphasize structure over agency, or dismiss legitimate concerns about social cohesion.

Conclusion: Why This Matters Beyond Academia

For critical theorists, recognizing conservatism’s role in maintaining oppression is not about "blaming conservatives." It is a diagnostic tool to:

  • Demystify power: Show how "common sense" ideas sustain inequality.
  • Empower action: Guide movements toward transformative (not piecemeal) change.
  • Honor resistance: Validate historical struggles that named conservatism as a barrier to justice.

This understanding is vital because systems of oppression cannot be undone by those who refuse to see their machinery. From a critical lens, justice requires dismantling the ideologies that make hierarchy feel inevitable—a task that begins with clear-eyed analysis. However, this perspective must be applied with nuance, avoiding reductionism while centering the goal of liberation. As bell hooks urged, critical work must always ask: "Who does this ideology serve?" The answer reveals whether "order" is truly just—or simply the peace of the graveyard.

Model Response:

Conservatism as the Ideology of Oppression: A Fundamental Critique

From the defense of monarchy against democratic revolutions to the modern backlash against racial justice, gender equality, and economic fairness, conservatism has served as the intellectual and political foundation of oppressive social hierarchies. Far from being a neutral or benign political philosophy, conservatism is fundamentally defined by its commitment to preserving and justifying systems of domination based on race, gender, and class. At its core, conservatism is not merely resistant to change—it is actively hostile to the dismantling of unequal power structures, using tradition, naturalized hierarchies, and appeals to order to maintain the subjugation of marginalized groups.

This essay argues that conservatism, in all its historical and contemporary forms, is inherently bound to the perpetuation of injustice. Whether in its classical Burelian defense of aristocracy, its modern neoliberal opposition to redistribution, or its socially reactionary resistance to civil rights, conservatism functions as the ideological bulwark of oppression. Any movement toward true liberation must necessarily reject conservatism in its entirety, for it is not a philosophy that can be reformed—it is one that must be abolished.

I. The Conservation of Oppression: Tradition as a Tool of Domination

Conservatism’s foundational principle is the veneration of tradition. Yet traditions are never neutral; they are the accumulated norms, institutions, and practices of those who have historically held power. When conservatives argue for the preservation of tradition, they are, in effect, arguing for the preservation of the power structures that produced those traditions. This is not an accidental feature of conservatism but its very essence.

Edmund Burke, the philosophical godfather of modern conservatism, did not merely critique the French Revolution on abstract grounds—he defended the aristocratic privileges it threatened. His famous metaphor of society as a contract "between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born" was, in practice, a defense of inherited power. The traditions he sought to conserve included the divine right of kings, the subjugation of women, and the brutalities of colonialism—all systems that benefited the elite at the expense of the many. Burke’s horror at revolution was not a disinterested concern for stability; it was the terror of a ruling class witnessing the unraveling of its own dominance.

This pattern persists today. The "traditional family" extolled by modern conservatives is a structure that has historically confined women to domestic spheres, denied LGBTQ+ people the right to exist openly, and reinforced patriarchal control over reproduction and sexuality. The "traditional" economic system of unfettered capitalism preserves class hierarchies by treating poverty as a personal failing rather than a structural inequality. And the "traditional" racial order—whether in the form of segregation, immigration restrictions, or mass incarceration—has consistently served to maintain white supremacy.

Tradition, in the conservative imagination, is not a living, evolving practice but a fixed ideal that must be defended against any challenge. This static view of tradition ensures that the oppressions of the past are perpetuated into the present and future. When conservatives decry "radical" changes like marriage equality, reparations for slavery, or universal healthcare, they are not defending abstract principles—they are defending the concrete inequalities that those traditions have long upheld. The appeal to tradition is not a call to preserve the best of the past; it is a demand to maintain the power structures that have always defined it.

II. Skepticism as a Weapon Against Justice

A second pillar of conservatism is its deep skepticism toward deliberate social reform. Conservative thinkers from Burke to Michael Oakeshott have argued that human attempts to rationally redesign society are hubristic and doomed to failure. In practice, this skepticism is selectively applied. While conservatives express caution about progressive reforms, they have shown no such hesitation in dismantling the social safety net, rolling back civil rights protections, or expanding the carceral state.

This skepticism is not a philosophical quirk but a political tool. It serves to delegitimize movements for equality by framing them as dangerous or unnatural. The Civil Rights Movement was dismissed as "moving too fast"; the feminist movement was (and is) derided as a threat to the natural order; and contemporary movements like Black Lives Matter are condemned as divisive and destructive. This skepticism is not applied to conservative policies that reinforce hierarchy. There is no conservative caution about the rapid expansion of executive power to crack down on protests, no hesitation in slashing taxes for the wealthy, no concern about the destabilizing effects of unchecked capitalism.

This selective skepticism reveals its true purpose: to maintain the status quo of inequality. When Martin Luther King Jr. wrote from Birmingham Jail that the "white moderate" who prefers "order over justice" is a greater obstacle to racial progress than the outright racist, he was describing the functional role of conservatism in maintaining oppression. The conservative does not need to be a bigot to uphold bigoted systems; they need only to insist that change is too risky, too fast, or too radical.

Consider the conservative response to the 1619 Project, which sought to reframe American history by centering the role of slavery and its legacy. Rather than engaging with the scholarship, conservatives across the political spectrum—from intellectuals to state legislators—moved to ban its teaching in schools. The justification? That it was "divisive," "unpatriotic," or "clidean." But the real objection was that it challenged the traditional narrative of American history, one that centers white, male, capitalist achievement and erases the violence of slavery, genocide, and exploitation. The conservative impulse is not to correct or complicate history, but to suppress any interpretation that threatens the mythologies that justify existing power structures.

III. Naturalizing Hierarchy: The Pseudoscience of Domination

Conservatism does not merely preserve existing hierarchies—it often seeks to justify them as natural, inevitable, or even divinely ordained. This naturalization of inequality is a recurring theme in conservative thought, providing a pseudo-intellectual veneer for oppression.

Burke spoke of a "natural aristocracy," implying that some were inherently suited to rule. In the American context, pro-slavery intellectuals like John C. Calhoun argued that slavery was a "positive good," not just for whites but even for the enslaved, who were said to benefit from the paternalistic care of their masters. This was not merely a defense of an economic system; it was an attempt to naturalize racial hierarchy as a moral and biological fact.

In the 20th century, conservatives opposed civil rights legislation on the grounds that racial segregation was the natural order of things. Today, the tradition continues. Charles Murray’s The Bell Curve (1994), widely celebrated in conservative intellectual circles, argued that racial differences in IQ were genetically determined, a claim thoroughly debunked by scientists but still repeated in conservative media. More recently, figures like Jordan Peterson have used pseudoscientific appeals to "biological reality" to oppose transgender rights, arguing that gender is an immutable, binary fact tied to chromosomes—ignoring the vast complexity of biological sex and the social construction of gender.

The function of these arguments is clear: if hierarchies are natural, then attempts to dismantle them are not just misguided but unnatural. This allows conservatives to oppose policies aimed at redressing inequality without having to confront the moral implications of their position. If poverty is the result of individual failure rather than structural inequity, then there is no need for wealth redistribution. If racial disparities in policing are the result of innate differences in criminality, then there is no need to reform the criminal justice system. If gender roles are biologically determined, then feminism is not a movement for liberation but a rebellion against nature itself.

This naturalization of hierarchy is not limited to race and gender. Economic conservatism, too, relies on a naturalized view of class. The idea that some people are "naturally" more talented, hardworking, or deserving than others is used to justify vast inequalities in wealth and power. The myth of meritocracy—that success is solely the result of individual effort and ability—serves to obscure the structural advantages and disadvantages that shape people’s lives. In this view, the wealthy deserve their wealth, and the poor deserve their poverty. Any attempt to redistribute wealth or power is thus framed as an unjust interference with the natural order of things.

IV. Order as a Code for Control

Another central tenet of conservatism is its emphasis on social order. Yet this order is not neutral or universally beneficial. It is an order that serves the interests of the powerful by suppressing dissent and maintaining control over marginalized groups.

The conservative preoccupation with "law and order" has consistently been used as a cudgel against racial justice movements. Richard Nixon’s 1968 campaign famously capitalized on white fears of Black urban uprisings, using coded language about "law and order" to appeal to racist sentiments. This strategy was not new—it was a continuation of a long tradition of using the specter of Black criminality to justify state violence and white supremacy. The same rhetoric was used to defend segregation, lynching, and the disenfranchisement of Black voters. Today, it is used to justify the militarization of police, the expansion of mass incarceration, and the suppression of protests against police brutality.

Similarly, conservative emphasis on order has been used to justify the policing of gender and sexuality. The criminalization of homosexuality, the regulation of women’s bodies through abortion bans, and the pathologization of gender nonconformity are all framed as necessary to maintain social stability. Yet what is being stabilized is not society as a whole, but a hierarchical system in which certain groups (white, male, straight, cisgender, wealthy) maintain dominance. When conservatives argue that marriage equality will lead to the collapse of society, they are not defending marriage—they are defending the patriarchal control over family structures that has long defined it.

This emphasis on order also extends to the workplace. Conservative opposition to labor unions, minimum wage laws, and worker protections is often framed as a defense of economic freedom. But in practice, it serves to maintain the power of capital over labor, ensuring that workers remain subdued and exploitable. The conservative vision of order is one in which the powerful are free to exercise their power without interference, while the marginalized are expected to accept their subordination. When workers strike for better wages or conditions, conservatives decry it as a disruption of order—never mind that the "order" being disrupted is one of exploitation.

The conservative obsession with order is, at its root, a fear of the oppressed. It is the recognition that the existing hierarchy is not natural or inevitable, but something that must be actively enforced. The calls for "civility" in the face of injustice, the demands for "unity" in the face of oppression, the insistence on "stability" in the face of change—all these are appeals to maintain the status quo, no matter how unjust it may be.

V. Property Above People: The Conservative Hierarchy of Rights

At the heart of economic conservatism is an almost sacrosanct reverence for property rights. Yet this reverence often comes at the expense of the rights of people, particularly those who are marginalized. In the conservative worldview, property rights are not just important—they are fundamental, often trumping other considerations of justice or equality.

Historically, this has had devastating consequences. The defense of property rights was used to justify slavery (as property in human beings) and colonialism (as the right to claim and exploit land and resources). The Three-Fifths Compromise in the U.S. Constitution, which counted enslaved Black people as three-fifths of a person for the purposes of representation, was a direct result of the prioritization of property rights (in this case, the "property" of slaveholders) over the rights of human beings. Similarly, the Dred Scott decision, which ruled that Black people could not be U.S. citizens, was rooted in the idea that the property rights of slaveholders took precedence over the humanity of the enslaved.

Today, this prioritization of property over people continues to shape conservative policy. Conservative opposition to policies like rent control, living wage laws, or universal healthcare is often framed as a defense of property rights. But what this really means is that the right of a landlord to charge exorbitant rent, or a corporation to pay poverty wages, takes precedence over the right of people to housing, food, or medical care. When conservatives argue that businesses should have the "freedom" to refuse service to LGBTQ+ people, they are prioritizing the property rights of business owners over the dignity and equality of marginalized groups.

This prioritization is not accidental but inherent to conservative ideology. The conservative belief in the sanctity of property rights is tied to a broader belief in the naturalness of inequality. If some people are naturally more deserving than others, then it follows that they should be allowed to accumulate more property—and that the state should protect their right to do so, even at the expense of others. This is why conservative economic policy so often serves to exacerbate inequality: tax cuts for the wealthy, deregulation of corporations, opposition to labor rights, and the gutting of social welfare programs are all justified in the name of protecting property rights.

The conservative emphasis on property rights also extends to the realm of ideas. The conservative backlash against "cancel culture" is often framed as a defense of free speech. Yet this "free speech" is selectively applied. Conservatives have shown little concern for the free speech rights of Black athletes protesting police brutality, or of professors teaching critical race theory, or of workers organizing unions. The conservative defense of free speech is not a principle but a weapon—one used to protect the speech of the powerful while suppressing the speech of the marginalized. In this sense, even intellectual property is subsumed under the broader conservative project of maintaining hierarchy.

VI. The Intersectionality of Conservative Oppression

The oppressions upheld by conservatism do not exist in isolation; they intersect and compound one another. A Black woman working a minimum wage job, for example, faces not only class oppression (as a worker) but also racial oppression (as a person of color in a racist society) and gender oppression (as a woman in a patriarchal system). Conservative policies often exacerbate all these forms of oppression simultaneously, creating a web of discrimination that is greater than the sum of its parts.

For instance, conservative opposition to minimum wage increases disproportionately affects women and people of color, who are overrepresented in low-wage jobs. According to the Economic Policy Institute, nearly two-thirds of workers earning the federal minimum wage of $7.25 per hour are women, and a disproportionate number are Black or Latina. When conservatives block minimum wage increases, they are not just upholding class inequality—they are reinforcing racial and gender inequalities as well.

Similarly, conservative attacks on voting rights disproportionately disenfranchise Black and brown communities, who are already marginalized in the political system. The gutting of the Voting Rights Act in 2013, for example, led to a wave of voter suppression laws—voter ID requirements, polling place closures, and purging of voter rolls—that disproportionately targeted communities of color. These laws are often justified in the name of preventing "voter fraud," a problem that has been shown to be virtually nonexistent. The real purpose is to maintain political power for white conservatives by suppressing the votes of those most likely to challenge their dominance.

Conservative opposition to reproductive rights also has intersectional implications. Abortion bans disproportionately affect low-income women, who may not have the resources to travel to states where abortion is legal or to access other forms of reproductive healthcare. Women of color are also disproportionately affected, as they are more likely to face barriers to healthcare access and more likely to be policed and criminalized for their reproductive choices. When conservatives argue that abortion is "murder," they ignore the fact that forcing someone to carry a pregnancy to term against their will is also a form of violence—one that is disproportionately borne by marginalized women.

This intersectionality is not a bug but a feature of conservative ideology. By upholding multiple, overlapping hierarchies, conservatism ensures that marginalized groups are divided and weakened, making it harder for them to challenge the system as a whole. A Black worker and a white worker may share class interests, but conservative rhetoric that blames immigrants or people of color for economic woes can drive a wedge between them. Similarly, a woman of color may face both sexism and racism, but conservative appeals to "family values" or "law and order" can pit her against other marginalized groups, such as LGBTQ+ people or undocumented immigrants.

VII. The Myth of "Compassionate Conservatism"

In the face of this damning indictment, some might argue that not all conservatism is oppressive—that there are forms of conservatism that seek to mitigate inequality without dismantling hierarchy. The most prominent example of this is "compassionate conservatism," a term popularized by George W. Bush in the 2000 presidential campaign. Bush and other proponents of this ideology argued that conservatism could be softened to accommodate concerns about poverty, education, and social welfare, all while maintaining a commitment to traditional values and free markets.

Yet a closer examination reveals that compassionate conservatism is little more than a rhetorical sleight of hand. It does not challenge the fundamental hierarchies that conservatism seeks to preserve; it merely seeks to make them slightly more bearable for those at the bottom. For example, Bush’s signature "compassionate conservative" policy, the No Child Left Behind Act, was framed as an effort to improve education for disadvantaged students. In practice, it led to increased standardized testing, the defunding of public schools, and the expansion of charter schools—policies that ultimately served to privatize education and undermine public institutions, rather than addressing the root causes of educational inequality.

Similarly, Bush’s faith-based initiatives provided some social services through religious organizations but did nothing to challenge the structural inequalities that create poverty in the first place. In fact, by outsourcing social services to religious groups, these initiatives often reinforced conservative moral values, such as opposition to abortion and LGBTQ+ rights, while doing little to address material deprivation.

Moreover, these reformist strands of conservatism are consistently undermined by the more reactionary elements of the movement. The Republican Party’s shift to the right under Donald Trump—with its open racism, misogyny, xenophobia, and authoritarianism—revealed the true nature of conservatism. When pressed, conservatives almost always retreat to the defense of hierarchy. The few moderate or "compassionate" conservatives who do exist are either co-opted by the reactionary mainstream or marginalized within the movement. The myth of compassionate conservatism is just that: a myth, a temporary tactic to make oppression more palatable, but never a genuine alternative to it.

Even in its most "moderate" forms, conservatism cannot escape its fundamental commitment to hierarchy. Consider the case of David Brooks, a New York Times columnist often held up as a "reasonable" conservative. While Brooks may express concern for the poor or sympathy for social justice causes, his solutions are always framed within a conservative worldview that prioritizes stability, tradition, and gradualism over radical change. His vision of a "good society" is one in which the poor are uplifted through moral and cultural reform, not through structural economic transformation. In other words, the problem is not inequality itself, but the supposed moral failings of those at the bottom. This is not a break from conservative ideology—it is a reiteration of its core tenets.

VIII. The Inevitability of Oppression Under Conservatism

Some may argue that conservatism is not inherently oppressive, but that it has simply been co-opted by extremists or misapplied in practice. Yet a closer look at the philosophy itself reveals that oppression is not a distortion of conservatism but its inevitable outcome.

Conservatism is, at its heart, a philosophy of preservation. It seeks to preserve existing institutions, traditions, and power structures. In a world characterized by deep and historically rooted inequalities, this means preserving those inequalities as well. There is no version of conservatism that does not, in some way, uphold the status quo—and in a status quo defined by racism, sexism, and classism, this means upholding those systems of oppression.

Even when conservatives claim to support equality, their vision of equality is almost always a formal, rather than substantive, one. Formal equality—the idea that everyone should have the same rights and opportunities in theory—does little to address the structural barriers that prevent marginalized groups from achieving true equality. Conservatives may argue that racial discrimination is wrong, but they oppose affirmative action, reparations, or other policies that seek to redress historical injustices. They may argue that women deserve equal pay, but they oppose policies like paid family leave or universal childcare that would make it possible for women to achieve economic equality. They may argue that everyone has the right to vote, but they support voter suppression laws that make it harder for marginalized groups to exercise that right.

This commitment to formal over substantive equality is not accidental. It reflects a fundamental conservative belief in the naturalness of hierarchy. If some people are naturally more talented, hardworking, or deserving than others, then formal equality—equal rights under the law—is enough. Any attempt to achieve substantive equality—actual parity in outcomes—is seen as an unjust interference with the natural order of things.

In this sense, conservatism is not just resistant to change—it is actively hostile to it. The conservative vision is not one of progress toward a more just society, but of stasis—a frozen moment in which existing hierarchies are preserved in amber. This is why conservative movements so often seem to be fighting a rear-guard action against history itself. From the resistance to abolition to the backlash against civil rights, from the opposition to women’s suffrage to the attacks on reproductive rights, conservatism has consistently positioned itself as the defender of the past against the demands of the future.

IX. Conclusion: Conservatism as the Enemy of Liberation

Conservatism is not merely a political ideology that sometimes upholds oppression; it is an ideology that is fundamentally defined by its commitment to preserving and justifying oppressive hierarchies. From its veneration of tradition to its skepticism toward reform, its naturalization of inequality to its emphasis on order and property, conservatism serves as the intellectual and political defense of systems of domination based on race, gender, and class.

This is not to say that all conservatives are conscious oppressors. Many conservatives are well-intentioned people who genuinely believe that their policies will lead to a better society. But good intentions do not change the fact that conservative ideology, by its very nature, serves to uphold injustice. The road to hell is paved with good intentions, and the history of conservatism is a testament to that truth.

The struggle for justice, then, requires more than just opposing individual conservative policies. It requires a fundamental rejection of conservatism as an ideology. True liberation cannot be achieved by working within the frameworks that conservatism provides, because those frameworks are designed to prevent liberation in the first place.

To build a just society, we must tear down the hierarchies that conservatism seeks to preserve—and that means tearing down conservatism itself. Any movement that seeks to dismantle oppressive systems of race, gender, and class must necessarily be opposed to conservatism in all its forms. There can be no compromise with an ideology whose very essence is the perpetuation of injustice. The choice is clear: either we accept the hierarchies that conservatism defends, or we reject conservatism and work toward a world free from oppression.
