Conservative ideology, in its myriad forms, presents itself as a commitment to tradition, order, and stability. Yet beneath this veneer lies a far more insidious truth: conservatism is fundamentally rooted in upholding oppressive social hierarchies based on race, gender, and class. At its core, conservatism seeks to preserve existing power structures, regardless of their inherent injustice, and it does so at the direct expense of marginalized groups. This essay will demonstrate that from its historical origins to its contemporary manifestations—including economic libertarianism, social traditionalism, and neoconservatism—conservative thought and policy are inextricably linked to the maintenance of inequality and the suppression of social progress.

The Historical Foundations of Hierarchical Preservation

Conservatism as a coherent political philosophy emerged in response to the radical egalitarianism of the French Revolution. Edmund Burke, often regarded as the father of modern conservatism, penned Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) as a dire warning against the dangers of upending established social order. Burke argued that society is an organic entity shaped by history and tradition, and that sudden attempts to impose equality would lead to chaos and tyranny. While he advocated for gradual reform, his primary concern was the preservation of hierarchy—specifically the monarchy, the aristocracy, and the established church. These institutions were, by design, oppressive: they concentrated power in the hands of a privileged few while denying basic rights to the majority.

Later conservative thinkers, such as Joseph de Maistre, were even more explicit. De Maistre asserted that hierarchy is natural and necessary, with the subordination of the many to the few being divinely ordained. This foundational belief—that society must be structured around inherited ranks and fixed roles—has permeated conservative thought ever since. In practice, this translates to a resistance to any change that threatens the status quo, especially when that change seeks to redistribute power to historically marginalized groups.

Class Hierarchies: The Economic Engine of Oppression

Economic conservatism, whether in the guise of free-market fundamentalism, supply-side economics, or austerity politics, is a primary vehicle for reinforcing class hierarchies. Conservatives champion policies that prioritize property rights and capital accumulation over the well-being of the working class and the poor. The result is a stark and growing economic divide that entrenches the power of elites while immiserating the masses.

The Reagan era offers a clear illustration. Reaganomics—marked by massive tax cuts for the wealthy, deregulation of industry, and union busting—was justified by the trickle-down myth that benefits for the rich would eventually reach everyone else. In reality, wealth inequality skyrocketed, real wages stagnated, and the social safety net was shredded. These outcomes were not accidental; they were the logical consequence of an ideology that views extreme wealth as a sign of virtue and poverty as a personal failing. By opposing progressive taxation, minimum wage increases, and robust labor protections, conservatives ensure that the capitalist class retains its dominant position.

Moreover, conservatives have consistently opposed organized labor, recognizing that unions empower workers to challenge the power imbalance between labor and capital. From the violent suppression of strikes in the early 20th century to the modern push for “right-to-work” laws, conservatives have worked tirelessly to weaken collective bargaining and keep wages low. This systematic assault on working-class power is a testament to conservatism’s commitment to class hierarchy.

Racial Hierarchies: White Supremacy in Conservative Garb

Conservatism’s relationship with racial oppression is equally damning. From the defense of slavery and segregation to the contemporary “Southern Strategy” and its descendants, conservative politics have been a bulwark of white supremacy in the United States and beyond.

During the Civil Rights Movement, conservatives were at the forefront of resistance. Barry Goldwater, the 1964 Republican presidential nominee, voted against the Civil Rights Act, and his campaign appealed to segregationist Democrats in the South. Richard Nixon’s “law and order” rhetoric and George H.W. Bush’s infamous Willie Horton ad stoked racial fears to win elections. Today, voter suppression laws—strict ID requirements, purges of voter rolls, and gerrymandering—disproportionately disenfranchise Black and Latino voters, effectively preserving white political dominance.

Criminal justice policies provide another glaring example. The “tough-on-crime” approach, championed by conservatives since the 1980s, has led to mass incarceration, with African Americans and Hispanics bearing the brunt of harsh sentencing and aggressive policing. The war on drugs, mandatory minimums, and private prisons have all served to criminalize communities of color while bolstering the prison-industrial complex.   • Strategic Guidance for Progressive Movements

  • Solidarity Building

  • Development of Critical Consciousness

Why This Understanding Is Crucial from a Critical Perspective

Critical theory aims not only to interpret the world but to change it. Its goal is emancipation from all forms of domination. Recognizing conservative ideology’s role in sustaining oppression is essential for several reasons:

  • Unmasking the Mechanisms of Domination
    Critical theory seeks to expose how power operates through culture and ideology. By dissecting conservatism, we illuminate one of the primary ways in which unjust hierarchies are legitimized and reproduced.

  • Demystifying the Social Order
    A core tenet of critical thought is that what appears natural is often historical and contingent. Conservative ideology reinforces the “naturalness” of inequality; deconstructing it reveals that society could be organized differently.

  • Enabling Praxis
    Praxis—reflective action aimed at liberation—requires an accurate understanding of the obstacles to justice. If conservatism is a major barrier, then efforts to dismantle it (through education, activism, and policy) become a priority.

  • Promoting Reflexivity
    Critical perspectives emphasize self‑reflection and the recognition of one’s own position within power structures. Recognizing conservatism’s function encourages individuals, even those who identify as conservative, to examine how their beliefs may unintentionally support oppression.

  • Fulfilling the Normative Commitment to Justice
    Ultimately, critical theory is driven by a normative commitment to equality and freedom. Exposing conservatism’s oppressive function is a step toward creating a society where those values are realized.

Caveats and Nuance

It is important to note that not every individual who identifies as conservative actively intends to oppress others. Ideology often operates at an unconscious level, and many people adopt conservative views out of genuine concern for stability or cultural continuity. However, from a structural perspective, the effect of these views—when dominant—is the preservation of hierarchies. Moreover, critical analysis does not dismiss all conservative ideas out of hand; it scrutinizes their social function within specific historical contexts.

Conclusion

From a critical standpoint, conservative ideology is not simply a political preference but a key instrument in maintaining social oppression and unjust hierarchies. The reasons for this view are grounded in history, theory, policy outcomes, rhetoric, institutional alignments, and cultural hegemony. Recognizing this function yields significant benefits: it demystifies power, enhances critical analysis, empowers the marginalized, informs progressive strategy, builds solidarity, and fosters critical consciousness. This understanding is indispensable for anyone committed to the critical project of unveiling and challenging the structures that perpetuate inequality, ultimately guiding us toward a more just and emancipated society.

At the heart of conservative thought lies a fundamental commitment to hierarchy. Conservatives do not deny inequality; they justify it. When enslaved people demanded freedom, conservatives codified chattel slavery in the U.S. Constitution through the Three-Fifths Compromise. And when labor unions won fair wages, conservatives branded them as threats to "business confidence" and worked to dismantle collective bargaining. Each reform that sought to redistribute power has been met with conservative resistance, revealing a pattern: conservatism resists correction, not because the corrections are flawed, but because the existing order is beneficial to those at the top—and that is the entire point.

The racial dimension of conservatism is perhaps the most transparently oppressive. History demonstrates that conservative movements have not merely tolerated racial hierarchies; they have actively created and defended them. The anti-abolitionist movement, Jim Crow laws, and modern voter suppression tactics all carry the conservative seal of approval. In the 20th century, conservative politicians deployed the “Southern Strategy,” a calculated effort to exploit racial resentment to consolidate white conservative voting blocs. Even today, conservative policies on crime, immigration, and welfare are uniquely punitive toward Black and Brown communities, reflecting not a concern for "law and order" but a desire to maintain racial control. The claim that colorblindness erases systemic racism is a conservative trick—a way to shift blame from institutions to individuals, ensuring that no one questions why some individuals are always under suspicion, always deemed ineligible.

Historically, conservatives opposed women’s education, justified marital rape as a husband’s right, and today support eroding access to contraception and abortion under the guise of “family values.” Such policies are not based on morality, but on the preservation of men’s power over women. When conservatives claim to honor “traditional roles,” they are not referencing an ideal past, but a regressive status quo where women’s labor, bodies, and choices are controlled by the state and their husbands. This is not preservation of culture; it is preservation of domination.

Class oppression is deeply embedded in conservative economic doctrine. Free-market fundamentalism—cherished by conservatives—is a myth used to rationalize extreme wealth concentration. 1. How Conservative Ideology Functions to Maintain Oppression

Conservative ideology (broadly defined as the defense of traditional power structures, hierarchy, and gradual or reactionary change) operates through several key mechanisms:

A. Naturalization of Hierarchy

    • Example: Poverty is framed as a personal flaw rather than a result of exploitative economic systems.

  • Moral Panics & Scapegoating: Conservatives frequently stigmatize marginalized groups (immigrants, racial minorities, LGBTQ+ people) to distract from economic or political failures.

    • Example: Anti-immigrant rhetoric ("they’re taking our jobs") obscures corporate exploitation of labor.

By preserving these hierarchies, conservatism inherently seeks to maintain unjust power structures, sacrificing the rights and well-being of marginalized groups.

At its inception, modern conservatism was a reaction to the rapid social changes that accompanied the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, and industrialization. These changes threatened the established order, which was built upon racial, gender, and class hierarchies. The early conservative thinker Edmund Burke famously argued for the preservation of traditional institutions and social relations, a stance that can be seen as a defense of the existing power structure (Burke, 1790). This initial commitment to the status quo set a precedent for conservatism's continued support of oppressive hierarchies.

Race has been a persistent factor in conservative ideology and policy. From the antebellum South to the present day, conservatives have often advocated for policies that disproportionately burden or exclude people of color. The right to vote, fair housing, and access to education have been historically restricted for racial minorities, with conservative resistance to their expansion. For instance, the Southern Strategy, a political appeasement of white segregationists by the Republican Party, highlights how conservatives have manipulated racist sentiments to gain political power (Perlstein, 2001). This strategy continues to influence conservative politics today, evident in anti-immigration policies, voter suppression laws, and the disproportionate policing of communities of color.

Gender is another axis of oppression that conservatism seeks to maintain. Conservatives have historically resisted women's rights, from suffrage to reproductive freedom. They have promoted traditional gender roles and family structures, often at the expense of women's autonomy and equality. The conservative perspective on abortion, which aims to restrict or abolish a woman's right to choose, is a prime example of how conservatism prioritizes certain ideologies over individual liberties and bodily autonomy (Fried, 2002). Similarly, conservatives often oppose measures to promote gender equality in the workplace and education, such as equal pay laws and gender-inclusive policies.

Furthermore, conservatism is inherently classist, as it frequently prioritizes the interests of the wealthy and privileged at the expense of the working class. Conservatives have historically opposed labor rights, regulations on business, and progressive taxation, policies which would benefit the working class (Domhoff, 2013). Additionally, conservative economic policies, such as trickle-down economics and austerity measures, often result in increased inequality and a further concentration of wealth in the hands of the elite. By preserving this class hierarchy, conservatism ensures that power remains in the hands of the few, while the many struggle with economic insecurity and diminished social mobility.

In conclusion, conservative ideology and political policy are deeply rooted in the preservation of oppressive social hierarchies based on race, gender, and class. By maintaining these unjust power structures, conservatism sacrifices the rights and well-being of marginalized groups. It is essential to critically examine and challenge these conservative values and policies to work towards a more just and equitable society.
